extracted.intended_audience: researchers and graduate students in constructive mathematics, logic, and computable analysis
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey of principles, theorems, and methodological criteria used in varieties of constructive mathematics and in constructive reverse mathematics (relations between BISH, INT, RUSS, ML, and CZF). Emphasises which nonclassical principles are necessary or equivalent to various constructive theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specker’s Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a strictly increasing sequence (r_1, r_2, ...) of rational numbers in the closed interval [0,1] such that for each x in R there exist N in N and δ > 0 such that |x - r_n| ≥ δ for all n ≥ N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a constructive (recursive) result showing behaviour different from classical expectations; used as an illustration of what can be deduced in RUSS and how classical intuitions about reals need reinterpretation in recursive/constructive settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive counterexamples in RUSS
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of recursive/constructive counterexamples: (1) a total function f : N×N → {0,1} with at most one n per m such that f(m,n)=1 and with the property that for each total g : N→{0,1} there exist m,k such that f(m,2k+g(m))=1; (2) for each ε>0 there exists an ε-singular cover of R (a sequence of bounded open intervals covering R with arbitrarily small finite initial sums); (3) existence of a pointwise continuous f : [0,1]→R that is not uniformly continuous; (4) existence of a positive-valued uniformly continuous f : [0,1]→R whose infimum is 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are used to show that LLPO and LPO are false in the recursive setting and to furnish strong recursive counterexamples to classical theorems (e.g., open-cover compactness and attainment of infimum). They illustrate how classical statements fail under recursive interpretations of 'function' and 'real number.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishop-style constructivism (BISH)
rubrics_metrics.description: A programme of constructive mathematics (BISH) developed by Errett Bishop which constructs large parts of analysis constructively using intuitionistic logic, without adopting Brouwer's non-classical principles or recursive function machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BISH emphasises readable, analyst-style mathematics that nonetheless is intuitionistic in logic. It admits many interpretations (INT, RUSS, classical) and practitioners typically follow the informal rules of constructive set- and function-construction given in Bishop [1967]. Criticism that it lacks logician-level precision can be addressed by observing that practice in BISH corresponds to working with intuitionistic logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martin-Löf’s constructive type theory (ML)
rubrics_metrics.description: A foundation for constructive mathematics where every proposition is represented as a type (propositions-as-types), proof objects witness propositions, and types are built by constructors (Π, Σ, products, disjoint unions, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes proof objects (witnesses) from derivations (records of construction). In ML every set is completely presented and the type-theoretic axiom of choice is derivable. The theory facilitates program extraction from proofs; practical implementations include Coq and Agda. When formalising reals one often uses setoids (types equipped with an equivalence relation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Full Axiom of Choice (classical statement) and its constructive interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Full AC: If A,B are inhabited sets and S⊆A×B satisfies ∀x∈A ∃y∈B ((x,y)∈S) then there exists a choice function f : A→B with ∀x∈A ((x,f(x))∈S). Constructively, the BHK interpretation requires an algorithm A which, given x and data proving x∈A, produces y∈B with (x,y)∈S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under constructive interpretation, full AC is problematic because f(x) may depend on the proof-data for x∈A; in ML (where sets are completely presented) the axiom of choice is derivable, but in Bishop-style mathematics full AC implies the law of excluded middle (Diaconescu–Goodman–Myhill), so constructive mathematicians commonly reject full AC while many accept countable choice and dependent choice. The text explains when AC can or cannot be expected to hold constructively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countable choice and dependent choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaker, often-accepted forms of choice in constructive mathematics: countable choice (choice with domain N) and dependent choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many constructive mathematicians accept countable and dependent choice for practical purposes, but some prefer to avoid even countable choice on philosophical grounds (speaking of an infinity of choices without giving a rule). Avoiding choice can exclude certain classical theorems as stated, forcing constructive reformulations (e.g., approximating the multiset of roots of a polynomial rather than separately approximating each root).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of exponentiation (constructive replacement for power set)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are sets then so is the set of all mappings from A into B. In particular, the class 2^N of all binary sequences is a set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the constructive alternative to the impredicative power set axiom, which many constructive mathematicians hesitate to accept. Forms the basis for discussing classes such as detachable subsets of N (dch(N)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detachable subsets and dch(N)
rubrics_metrics.description: dch(N) ≡ {S ⊆ N : ∀x∈N (x∈S ∨ x∉S)} is the class of detachable subsets of N. Constructively, dch(N) is equinumerous with 2^N and (using replacement in CZF) is a set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classically every subset of N is detachable, but constructively this fails; if all such subsets were detachable one could derive LEM. dch(N) is used to formulate a constructive version of the Continuum Hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive Continuum Hypothesis (CH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive CH: ∀C( N ≲ C ≲ dch(N) ∧ ¬(C ≅ N) ⇒ C ≅ dch(N) ). (Equivalently stated with a weaker classical-like formulation also given.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text sketches how CH implies the law of excluded middle constructively and analyses consequences when CH is taken as p in the argument (showing existence of a nonempty set X for which a member cannot be constructed). Formalisation is possible in CZF, and independence results (Gödel–Cohen) are discussed in relation to constructive interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive Reverse Mathematics (CRM) methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: CRM seeks to classify theorems according to which constructive set- or type-theoretic principles must be added to BISH to prove them. It has two parts: (1) for a theorem T of INT or RUSS, find a principle valid in that model which is necessary and sufficient to add to BISH to prove T; (2) for a classical theorem T suspected nonconstructive, prove T equivalent over BISH to a known nonconstructive principle (e.g., MP, LLPO, LPO, LEM).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical approach in CRM is informal (BISH-style). A common proof strategy constructs ?-subsets of 2^* from given data so that pointwise-to-uniform transitions correspond to bar-uniformity statements; conversely, given bars one constructs corresponding sets S. The programme is illustrated with fan-theorem equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: c-subset and Π^0_1-subset of 2^*
rubrics_metrics.description: A c-subset B of 2^* is of the form B = {u∈2^* : ∀v∈2^* (u^⌢v ∈ D)} for some detachable D ⊆ 2^*. A Π^0_1-subset B of 2^* is defined by the existence of a detachable S ⊆ 2^*×N with a hereditary property and B = {u : ∀n∈N ((u,n)∈S)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every detachable subset of 2^* is a c-subset, and every c-subset is a Π^0_1-subset (take S = D×N). These notions are used to formulate restricted forms of the fan theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan theorems: FT_D, FT_c, FT_{Π^0_1}, and FT
rubrics_metrics.description: FT_? (fan theorem for ?-bars): every bar with property ? is a uniform bar. Special cases: FT_D: every detachable bar of the complete binary fan is uniform; FT_c: every c-bar is uniform; FT_{Π^0_1}: every Π^0_1-bar is uniform; FT: every bar is uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative to BISH, FT ⇒ FT_{Π^0_1} ⇒ FT_c ⇒ FT_D and these implications are strict (Lubarsky & Diener). The fan theorems are central objects in CRM to which many analytic pointwise-to-uniform statements are equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity principle (POS)
rubrics_metrics.description: POS: Each positive-valued, uniformly continuous function on [0,1] has a positive infimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Julian & Richman proved that, relative to BISH, FT_D is equivalent to POS by constructing detachable subsets B of 2^* corresponding to uniformly continuous functions. POS is derivable in INT (where full FT holds) but fails in RUSS (where counterexamples exist). POS is also related/equivalent to FT_c via other work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Julian–Richman theorems (connection between bars and positivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 1: Given uniformly continuous f:[0,1]→R there exists a detachable subset B of 2^* such that if f(x)>0 for each x then B is a bar, and if B is a uniform bar then inf f > 0. Theorem 2: Given detachable B⊆2^* there exists uniformly continuous f with similar implications (B bar ⇒ f(x)>0 for each x; inf f>0 ⇒ B uniform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two theorems together show the equivalence of FT_D and POS over BISH; proofs are subtle and technical (see Julian & Richman [1984]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique-existence principles chain (CIN!, MIN!, WKL!, FIX!)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four principles of the form 'if there is at most one object with property P, then there is one such object': CIN!: Cantor intersection theorem with uniqueness for descending sequences of inhabited closed located subsets of a compact metric space; MIN!: Each uniformly continuous real-valued function on a compact metric space with at most one minimum point has a minimum point; WKL!: Weak König lemma with uniqueness (each infinite tree with at most one infinite branch has an infinite branch); FIX!: Each uniformly continuous map on a compact metric space with at most one fixed point and with approximate fixed points has a fixed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berger & Ishihara established a chain of equivalences between POS, FT_c, and variants of these unique-existence principles, showing how positivity and fan theorems translate into unique-existence existence results in compact metric spaces and combinatorial tree principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform Continuity Theorem for [0,1] (UCT_{[0,1]})
rubrics_metrics.description: UCT_{[0,1]}: Every pointwise continuous mapping of [0,1] into R is uniformly continuous (equivalently, the general uniform continuity theorem for complete, totally bounded metric spaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally proved by Brouwer using the fan theorem. In CRM, a major open problem is to identify a version of the fan theorem equivalent over BISH to UCT_{[0,1]}. Known results: BISH ⊢ UCT_{[0,1]} ⇒ FT_c (Berger) and BISH ⊢ FT_{Π^0_1} ⇒ UCT_{[0,1]} (Diener & Loeb), but bi-implications remain open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program extraction from constructive proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Every constructive proof embodies an algorithm that can in principle be extracted and recast as a computer program; the constructive proof itself verifies the algorithm meets its specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martin-Löf type theory particularly facilitates extraction; implementations and tools include Coq and Agda. This practical connection motivates constructive developments and formalisation efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of rejecting countable choice on constructive theorems (example: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra)
rubrics_metrics.description: Without countable choice one cannot in general construct separate approximations to each root of a polynomial, but one can construct arbitrarily close approximations to the multiset of roots (Richman [2000]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoiding choice forces reformulation of theorems to more constructive-friendly statements (e.g., focusing on approximate linear factorizations rather than individual roots). This is cited as an argument that avoiding choice can lead to better formulations.
